claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection in the Golden Syrian hamster causes lung pathology that resembles human coronavirus disease (COVID-19).
source: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection in the Golden Syrian hamster causes lung pathology that resembles human coronavirus disease (COVID-19).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding that provides context for the study.

claim: The early phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection in hamsters leads to an acute inflammatory response and lung pathologies.
source: Here, we show, using a hamster model, that the early phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection leads to an acute inflammatory response and lung pathologies
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The late phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection in hamsters causes cardiovascular complications characterized by ventricular wall thickening.
source: while the late phase of infection causes cardiovascular complications (CVCs) characterized by ventricular wall thickening associated with increased ventricular mass/body mass ratio and interstitial coronary fibrosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by histological data and measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters showed elevated levels of serum cardiac troponin I.
source: Molecular profiling further substantiated our findings of CVC as SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters showed elevated levels of serum cardiac troponin I, cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein, and long-chain fatty acid triglycerides.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA measurements of serum cardiac troponin I levels presented in Figure 3E.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters showed elevated levels of cholesterol.
source: Molecular profiling further substantiated our findings of CVC as SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters showed elevated levels of serum cardiac troponin I, cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein, and long-chain fatty acid triglycerides.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters showed elevated levels of low-density lipoprotein.
source: Molecular profiling further substantiated our findings of CVC as SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters showed elevated levels of serum cardiac troponin I, cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein, and long-chain fatty acid triglycerides.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters showed elevated levels of long-chain fatty acid triglycerides.
source: Molecular profiling further substantiated our findings of CVC as SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters showed elevated levels of serum cardiac troponin I, cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein, and long-chain fatty acid triglycerides.
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data showing increased LCFA TGs in infected hamsters.

claim: N-acetylneuraminate was found to be a common metabolic marker between SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters and COVID-19 patients.
source: Serum metabolomics profiling of SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters identified N-acetylneuraminate, a functional metabolite found to be associated with CVC, as a metabolic marker was found to be common between SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters and COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is supported by comparative metabolomics analysis between hamster and human COVID-19 samples presented in Figure 6.

claim: N-acetylneuraminate is associated with cardiovascular complications.
source: Serum metabolomics profiling of SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters identified N-acetylneuraminate, a functional metabolite found to be associated with CVC
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Maciel et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018) linking N-acetylneuraminate to coronary artery disease and myocardial injury.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 has infected nearly 0.9% of the total world population with a mortality rate of around 1.96% as of December 2021.
source: First reported in Wuhan, China, in December 2019, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) has infected nearly 0.9% of the total world population with a mortality rate of around 1.96% as of December 2021 (https://COVID-19.who.int/).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to WHO COVID-19 data.

claim: Symptomatic COVID-19 is typically characterized by symptoms ranging from mild to acute respiratory distress associated with cytokine release syndrome.
source: Symptomatic COVID-19 is typically characterized by symptoms ranging from mild to acute respiratory distress associated with cytokine release syndrome (Chen and Li, 2020; Verity et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Chen and Li, 2020; Verity et al., 2020).

claim: Extrapulmonary signs including cardiovascular complication, coagulopathies, multiple-organ damage, and neurological disorders were recognized as post-COVID sequelae in patients with mild to severe COVID-19.
source: Moreover, extrapulmonary signs, ranging from cardiovascular complication (CVC), coagulopathies, multiple-organ damage, and neurological disorders, were found to be recognized as post-COVID sequelae described in patients with mild to severe COVID-19 (Chen and Li, 2020; Cortinovis et al., 2021; Francis et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2021; Lamers et al., 2020; Mao et al., 2020; Neurath, 2020; Nishiga et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020b; Xiao et al., 2020; Xydakis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The severity of COVID-19 is governed by several factors such as titer of virus, route of viral entry, gender, age, and comorbid conditions.
source: The severity of COVID-19 is governed by several factors such as titer of virus, route of viral entry, gender, age, and comorbid conditions (Chen and Li, 2020; Sungnak et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Chen and Li, 2020; Sungnak et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020).

claim: The receptor-binding domain (RBD) of the spike (S) glycoprotein of SARS-CoV-2 engages with angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), a cellular receptor expressed primarily on host lung epithelial cells, which facilitates viral entry into the host cell.
source: The receptor-binding domain (RBD) of the spike (S) glycoprotein of SARS-CoV-2 engages with angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), a cellular receptor expressed primarily on host lung epithelial cells, which facilitates viral entry into the host cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 viral entry mechanism.

claim: Cellular transmembrane protease 'serine 2' (TMPRSS2) and neuropilin-1 (NRP-1) assist in the cellular entry of SARS-CoV-2.
source: In addition, other factors such as cellular transmembrane protease 'serine 2' (TMPRSS2) and neuropilin-1 (NRP-1) assist in the cellular entry of SARS-CoV-2 (Cantuti-Castelvetri et al., 2020; Daly et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Cantuti-Castelvetri et al., 2020; Daly et al., 2020).

claim: The Golden Syrian hamster was previously described as a model for SARS-CoV infection.
source: The Golden Syrian hamster, which was previously described as a model for SARS-CoV infection, has gained much attention as a suitable model for studying SARS-CoV-2 infection (Chan et al., 2020; Imai et al., 2020; Kaptein et al., 2020; Kreye et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020; Osterrieder et al., 2020; Rosenke et al., 2020; Sia et al., 2020; Tostanoski et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hamsters have been shown to be infected through intranasal, oral, and ophthalmic routes by SARS-CoV-2 with respectively descending lung viral load and pathologies.
source: Remarkably, hamsters have been shown to be infected through intranasal, oral, and ophthalmic routes by SARS-CoV-2 with respectively descending lung viral load and pathologies (Imai et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Imai et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020).

claim: The overlay of the crystal structure of huACE2 with modeled haACE2 was 1.2 Å, indicating high structural resemblance.
source: The overlay of the crystal structure of huACE2 with modeled haACE2 was 1.2 Å, indicating the high structural resemblance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by in silico molecular modeling data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: At the interface, 20 residues of hu ACE2 interact with 17 residues of RBD.
source: At the interface, 20 residues of hu ACE2 interact with 17 residues of RBD while 20 residues of ha ACE2 interact with 16 residues of RBD (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by molecular docking analysis presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 20 residues of ha ACE2 interact with 16 residues of RBD.
source: At the interface, 20 residues of hu ACE2 interact with 17 residues of RBD while 20 residues of ha ACE2 interact with 16 residues of RBD (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by molecular docking analysis presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The NRP-1 receptor binds to S1 fragment of the spike protein and facilitates SARS-CoV-2 entry into cells.
source: The NRP-1 receptor, which binds to S1 fragment of the spike protein and facilitates SARS-CoV-2 entry into cells (Cantuti-Castelvetri et al., 2020; Daly et al., 2020), also showed identical interaction with S1 fragment residues between hu and ha (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–I).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Cantuti-Castelvetri et al., 2020; Daly et al., 2020).

claim: NRP-1 showed identical interaction with S1 fragment residues between human and hamster.
source: The NRP-1 receptor, which binds to S1 fragment of the spike protein and facilitates SARS-CoV-2 entry into cells (Cantuti-Castelvetri et al., 2020; Daly et al., 2020), also showed identical interaction with S1 fragment residues between hu and ha (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–I).
evidence: This is supported by molecular modeling data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hamsters challenged with either 104 or 105 plaque-forming unit (PFU) SARS-CoV-2 showed a gradual decrease in body weight up to 4 dpi, and subsequently recovered.
source: In line with this, our data showed that hamsters challenged with either 104 or 105 plaque-forming unit (PFU) SARS-CoV-2 showed a gradual decrease in body weight up to 4 dpi, and subsequently recovered.
evidence: This is supported by body weight measurements presented in Figure 1A.

claim: The body weight loss in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters peaked (~10% as compared to uninfected) at 4 dpi.
source: The body weight loss peaked (~10% as compared to uninfected) at 4 dpi when compared to the unchallenged control hamsters (Figure 1A; Chan et al., 2020; Imai et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020; Sia et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by body weight measurements presented in Figure 1A and citations to previous studies.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-infected hamster lungs showed gross morphological changes characterized by pneumonitis regions.
source: This data was accompanied by gross lung morphological changes characterized by pneumonitis regions with a high lung viral copy number and TCID50 at 2 dpi that gradually decreased with disease progression, marking the recovery of the animals from SARS-CoV-2 infection (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by gross morphology images and viral load data presented in Figure 1B and C.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-infected hamster lungs showed high lung viral copy number and TCID50 at 2 dpi that gradually decreased with disease progression.
source: This data was accompanied by gross lung morphological changes characterized by pneumonitis regions with a high lung viral copy number and TCID50 at 2 dpi that gradually decreased with disease progression, marking the recovery of the animals from SARS-CoV-2 infection (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by viral load measurements presented in Figure 1C.

claim: COVID-19 is marked by severe pneumonia, lung injury, and an influx of activated immune cells.
source: COVID-19 is marked by severe pneumonia, lung injury, and an influx of activated immune cells (Afrin et al., 2020; Boudewijns et al., 2020; Chen and Li, 2020; Moore and June, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Afrin et al., 2020; Boudewijns et al., 2020; Chen and Li, 2020; Moore and June, 2020).

claim: Histological analysis of SARS-CoV-2-infected hamster lungs indicated an elevated disease index score marked by high scores of inflammation, epithelial injury, lung injury, and pneumonitis with elevated infiltration of granulocytes and mast cells on 2, 4, and 7 dpi.
source: In line with this, the histological analysis indicated an elevated disease index score marked by high scores of inflammation, epithelial injury, lung injury, and pneumonitis with elevated infiltration of granulocytes and mast cells on 2, 4, and 7 dpi (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by histological images and scoring data presented in Figure 1D and E.

claim: mRNA expression of mast cell signature enzymes, chymase and tryptase, was increased on 2 and 4 dpi in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters.
source: Consistently, mRNA expression of mast cell signature enzymes, chymase and tryptase (Caughey, 2007), was increased on 2 and 4 dpi corroborating with mast cell enrichment (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 1F and a citation to Caughey, 2007.

claim: The expression of eotaxin was upregulated at 2 dpi in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters.
source: Furthermore, the expression of eotaxin, a CC chemokine and a potent chemoattractant for airway eosinophils and mast cells found to be increased in asthma and allergy conditions, was upregulated at 2 dpi (Figure 1G; Guo et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 1G and a citation to Guo et al., 2001.

claim: Eotaxin is a CC chemokine and a potent chemoattractant for airway eosinophils and mast cells found to be increased in asthma and allergy conditions.
source: Furthermore, the expression of eotaxin, a CC chemokine and a potent chemoattractant for airway eosinophils and mast cells found to be increased in asthma and allergy conditions, was upregulated at 2 dpi (Figure 1G; Guo et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Guo et al., 2001.

claim: The expression of mucin (muc-1), surfactant protein-D (sftp-D), advanced glycation end product (AGER), and plasminogen activator inhibitor 1 (PAI-1) was upregulated at 4 dpi in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters.
source: The expression of other lung injury markers like mucin (muc-1: marker of respiratory infections), surfactant protein-D (sftp-D: acute lung injury marker), advanced glycation end product (AGER: pro-inflammatory pattern recognition receptor), and plasminogen activator inhibitor 1 (PAI-1: a key factor for lung fibrosis) was upregulated at 4 dpi (Figure 1G; Chatterjee et al., 2020; Crouch, 2000; Oczypok et al., 2017; Prabhakaran et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 1G and citations to previous studies.

claim: Mucin (muc-1) is a marker of respiratory infections.
source: The expression of other lung injury markers like mucin (muc-1: marker of respiratory infections), surfactant protein-D (sftp-D: acute lung injury marker), advanced glycation end product (AGER: pro-inflammatory pattern recognition receptor), and plasminogen activator inhibitor 1 (PAI-1: a key factor for lung fibrosis) was upregulated at 4 dpi (Figure 1G; Chatterjee et al., 2020; Crouch, 2000; Oczypok et al., 2017; Prabhakaran et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Surfactant protein-D (sftp-D) is an acute lung injury marker.
source: The expression of other lung injury markers like mucin (muc-1: marker of respiratory infections), surfactant protein-D (sftp-D: acute lung injury marker), advanced glycation end product (AGER: pro-inflammatory pattern recognition receptor), and plasminogen activator inhibitor 1 (PAI-1: a key factor for lung fibrosis) was upregulated at 4 dpi (Figure 1G; Chatterjee et al., 2020; Crouch, 2000; Oczypok et al., 2017; Prabhakaran et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Advanced glycation end product (AGER) is a pro-inflammatory pattern recognition receptor.
source: The expression of other lung injury markers like mucin (muc-1: marker of respiratory infections), surfactant protein-D (sftp-D: acute lung injury marker), advanced glycation end product (AGER: pro-inflammatory pattern recognition receptor), and plasminogen activator inhibitor 1 (PAI-1: a key factor for lung fibrosis) was upregulated at 4 dpi (Figure 1G; Chatterjee et al., 2020; Crouch, 2000; Oczypok et al., 2017; Prabhakaran et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Plasminogen activator inhibitor 1 (PAI-1) is a key factor for lung fibrosis.
source: The expression of other lung injury markers like mucin (muc-1: marker of respiratory infections), surfactant protein-D (sftp-D: acute lung injury marker), advanced glycation end product (AGER: pro-inflammatory pattern recognition receptor), and plasminogen activator inhibitor 1 (PAI-1: a key factor for lung fibrosis) was upregulated at 4 dpi (Figure 1G; Chatterjee et al., 2020; Crouch, 2000; Oczypok et al., 2017; Prabhakaran et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lung injury and multiple-organ failure have been attributed to the acute release of inflammatory cytokines caused by SARS-CoV-2 infection in COVID-19 patients.
source: Lung injury and multiple-organ failure have been attributed to the acute release of inflammatory cytokines caused by SARS-CoV-2 infection in COVID-19 patients (Iwasaki and Yang, 2020; Mathew et al., 2020; Moore and June, 2020; Verity et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Iwasaki and Yang, 2020; Mathew et al., 2020; Moore and June, 2020; Verity et al., 2020).

claim: SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters showed profound splenomegaly with an increase in spleen mass to body mass ratio at 2 and 4 dpi as compared to the uninfected animals.
source: We observed a profound splenomegaly in hamsters challenged with SARS-CoV-2 with an increase in spleen mass to body mass ratio at 2 and 4 dpi as compared to the uninfected animals (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by spleen measurements and images presented in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Splenomegaly subsided at the late phase of infection (7 and 14 dpi) in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters.
source: As hamsters recover from SARS- CoV-2 infection indicated by gain of body weight, splenomegaly also subsided at the late phase of infection (7 and 14 dpi), which is corroborated with recovery in lung pathologies (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by spleen measurements presented in Figure 2A.

claim: A high dose of SARS-CoV-2 infection generates a higher IgG titer against RBD compared to a low dose.
source: As compared to a low dose, a high dose of infection generates a higher IgG titer against RBD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The RBD, spike (prefusion S2P), and N protein ELISA detected the corresponding antibodies in challenged animals as early as 7 dpi.
source: The RBD, spike (prefusion S2P), and N protein ELISA detected the corresponding antibodies in challenged animals as early as 7 dpi.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: The serum endpoint antibody titers against RBD, spike, and N protein were 1:3610, 1:405, and 1:330, respectively, at 7 dpi for 105 PFU SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: The serum endpoint antibody titers against RBD, spike, and N protein were 1:3610, 1:405, and 1:330, respectively, and the titer of these antibodies was further enhanced to 1:8900, 1:550, and 1:660 at 14 dpi for PFU SARS-CoV-2 infection (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: The titer of antibodies against RBD, spike, and N protein was further enhanced to 1:8900, 1:550, and 1:660 at 14 dpi for 105 PFU SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: The serum endpoint antibody titers against RBD, spike, and N protein were 1:3610, 1:405, and 1:330, respectively, and the titer of these antibodies was further enhanced to 1:8900, 1:550, and 1:660 at 14 dpi for PFU SARS-CoV-2 infection (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: The frequency of RBD-specific CD4+IFNγ+ cells was elevated (~2.5-fold) in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters.
source: The cellular response was corroborated with the antibody response as the frequency of RBD-specific CD4+IFNγ+ cells was also found to be elevated (~2.5-fold) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters showed increased mRNA expression of signature cytokines of Th1 (IFNγ, TNF-α), Th2 (IL-13), Th9 (IL-9), and Th17 (IL-17A) cells and IL-6 cytokine at the peak of infection (i.e., 2 dpi).
source: Our data demonstrated an increased mRNA expression of signature cytokines of Th1 (IFNγ, tumor necrosis factor [TNF)-α], Th2(interleukin [IL]-13), Th9 (IL-9), and Th17 (IL-17A) cells and IL-6 cytokine at the peak of infection (i.e., 2 dpi) along with their respective transcription factors, T-bet, GATA3, and RAR-related orphan receptor (ROR)-c (de Candia et al., 2021; Grifoni et al., 2020; Mathew et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 2E and citations to previous studies.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters showed increased mRNA expression of transcription factors T-bet, GATA3, and ROR-c at 2 dpi.
source: Our data demonstrated an increased mRNA expression of signature cytokines of Th1 (IFNγ, tumor necrosis factor [TNF)-α], Th2(interleukin [IL]-13), Th9 (IL-9), and Th17 (IL-17A) cells and IL-6 cytokine at the peak of infection (i.e., 2 dpi) along with their respective transcription factors, T-bet, GATA3, and RAR-related orphan receptor (ROR)-c (de Candia et al., 2021; Grifoni et al., 2020; Mathew et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 2F and citations to previous studies.

claim: The transcription factor Foxp-3 was found to be elevated at 14 dpi in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters.
source: However, the transcription factor forkhead box protein (Foxp)-3 was found to be elevated at 14 dpi, suggesting a suppressive immunological response induced by regulatory T (Tregs) cells was increased with the declining of the infection.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 2F.

claim: Anti-inflammatory cytokines, IL-10 and TGF-β, were elevated at 2 dpi in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters.
source: Interestingly, anti-inflammatory cytokines, IL-10, and transforming growth factor (TGF)-β, set in much early at 2 dpi, which could serve to counterbalance an aggressive inflammatory reaction (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 2E and F.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters showed elevated expression of inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) at 2 dpi compared to uninfected hamsters.
source: We also found elevated expression of inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) at 2 dpi compared to uninfected hamsters, indicating a possible role of an oxidative environment in SARS-CoV-2-induced pathologies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters showed elevated expression of CCR5 and CCL-5 at 2 dpi.
source: We found elevated expression of C-C chemokine receptor (CCR5) and C-C motif chemokine ligand (CCL)-5 at 2 dpi, which are known to regulate T cell function and chemotaxis.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 2G.

claim: CCR5 and CCL-5 are known to regulate T cell function and chemotaxis.
source: We found elevated expression of C-C chemokine receptor (CCR5) and C-C motif chemokine ligand (CCL)-5 at 2 dpi, which are known to regulate T cell function and chemotaxis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CCR5 and CCL-5 function.

claim: CCL-22 was found to be elevated at 7 dpi in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters.
source: CCL-22, which is essential for Treg-dendritic cell (DC) cross-talk, was found to be elevated at 7 dpi as compared to uninfected hamsters.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 2G.

claim: CCL-22 is essential for Treg-dendritic cell (DC) cross-talk.
source: CCL-22, which is essential for Treg-dendritic cell (DC) cross-talk, was found to be elevated at 7 dpi as compared to uninfected hamsters.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CCL-22 function.

claim: The expression of CXCL9 and CXCL-10 was upregulated at 2 dpi in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters.
source: The expression of CXCL9 and CXCL-10, which are crucial for effector T cell trafficking and activation, and have been described as one of the biomarkers for CVC, was upregulated at 2 dpi as compared to uninfected hamsters (Figure 2G; Altara et al., 2016; Hueso et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 2G and citations to previous studies.

claim: CXCL9 and CXCL-10 are crucial for effector T cell trafficking and activation.
source: The expression of CXCL9 and CXCL-10, which are crucial for effector T cell trafficking and activation, and have been described as one of the biomarkers for CVC, was upregulated at 2 dpi as compared to uninfected hamsters (Figure 2G; Altara et al., 2016; Hueso et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Altara et al., 2016; Hueso et al., 2018).

claim: CXCL9 and CXCL-10 have been described as one of the biomarkers for CVC.
source: The expression of CXCL9 and CXCL-10, which are crucial for effector T cell trafficking and activation, and have been described as one of the biomarkers for CVC, was upregulated at 2 dpi as compared to uninfected hamsters (Figure 2G; Altara et al., 2016; Hueso et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Altara et al., 2016; Hueso et al., 2018).

claim: mRNA expression of PD-1 and its ligand, PDL-1, was found to be upregulated at the onset of infection in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters.
source: In addition, mRNA expression of PD-1 and its ligand, PDL-1, was found to be upregulated at the onset of infection, suggesting the induction of checkpoints to suppress the acute immune response induced by SARS-CoV-2 infection (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 2H.

claim: Myocardial injury is marked in around 25% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients.
source: Myocardial injury is marked in around 25% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients, which includes thromboembolic diseases and cases of arrhythmia (Giustino et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2020; Nishiga et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Giustino et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2020; Nishiga et al., 2020).

claim: 7 and 14 dpi hearts of SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters showed clear ventricular hypertrophy, marked by a significant increase in ventricular mass to body mass ratio.
source: Indeed, 7 and 14 dpi hearts showed clear ventricular hypertrophy, marked by a significant increase in ventricular mass to body mass ratio in challenged hamsters as compared to unchallenged hamsters (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by heart measurements presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The ventricular space was reduced as characterized by thickening of the ventricular wall and interventricular septum at 7 and 14 dpi in SARS-CoV-2-challenged hamsters.
source: It was further observed that the ventricular space was reduced as characterized by thickening of the ventricular wall and interventricular septum at 7 and 14 dpi in SARS-CoV-2-challenged hamsters as compared to uninfected controls (Figure 3A and D).
evidence: This is supported by histological images and scoring data presented in Figure 3A and D.

claim: The ventricular wall thickening at 7 and 14 dpi with SARS-CoV-2 infection in the hamster was marked by increased inflammation surrounding the coronary artery and elevated interstitial coronary fibrosis.
source: The ventricular wall thickening at 7 and 14 dpi with SARS-CoV-2 infection in the hamster was marked by increased inflammation surrounding the coronary artery and elevated interstitial coronary fibrosis (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by histological images and scoring data presented in Figure 3B–D.

claim: Increased fibrosis is an established pathophysiological stage in the majority of CVC.
source: Interestingly, increased fibrosis is an established pathophysiological stage in the majority of CVC (Kong et al., 2014; Travers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Kong et al., 2014; Travers et al., 2016).

claim: There was a gradual increase in serum cardiac troponin I (cTnI) levels from the early to late phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection in hamsters.
source: There was a gradual increase in serum cardiac troponin I (cTnI) levels from the early to late phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection in hamsters (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: Remdesivir was able to inhibit serum cTnI levels at 4 dpi when compared to the infection control.
source: Remarkably, remdesivir, which has been shown to have significant antiviral efficacy in hamsters, was able to inhibit serum cTnI levels at 4 dpi when compared to the infection control (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; Cortinovis et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and a citation to Cortinovis et al., 2021.

claim: Remdesivir has been shown to have significant antiviral efficacy in hamsters.
source: Remarkably, remdesivir, which has been shown to have significant antiviral efficacy in hamsters, was able to inhibit serum cTnI levels at 4 dpi when compared to the infection control (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; Cortinovis et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cortinovis et al., 2021.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters showed elevated serum IL-6 levels at 2 dpi.
source: We also found elevated serum IL-6 levels at 2 dpi (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 3F.

claim: IL-6 is used as a prognosis marker for CVC.
source: In addition to inflammation indicator, IL-6 is used as a prognosis marker for CVC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IL-6 as a biomarker.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection increases serum levels of IL-6, which decreases during later time points of infection.
source: Our data indicated that SARS-CoV-2 infection increases serum levels of IL-6 ,which decreases during later time points of infection (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: There was a high viral load in the heart of infected hamsters at 2 dpi as compared to uninfected controls.
source: The elevated levels of CVC markers were accompanied by a high viral load in the heart of infected hamsters at 2 dpi as compared to uninfected controls (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 3G.

claim: The viral load in the heart was significantly reduced with remdesivir administration.
source: The viral load in the heart was significantly reduced with remdesivir administration and was in line with reduced cTnI levels during infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: No significant viral load was found in the heart at 7 and 14 dpi in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters.
source: Interestingly, we did not find any significant viral load in the heart at 7 and 14 dpi.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 3G.

claim: CVCs are often linked with a perturbed serum lipid profile.
source: Since CVCs are often linked with a perturbed serum lipid profile, we reasoned that cardiovascular pathologies of SARS-CoV-2 in hamsters may be related to changes in circulating lipid molecules (Bruzzone et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Bruzzone et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020a).

claim: The serum lipid profile of SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters showed elevated cholesterol, TGs, HDLs, LDLs, and VLDL levels at 4 dpi.
source: Indeed, the serum lipid profile showed elevated cholesterol, TGs, HDLs, LDLs, and very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) levels at 4 dpi (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: LC-MS/MS data identified 831 lipid molecules from the hamster serum samples.
source: Our LC-MS/MS data identified 831 lipid molecules from the hamster serum samples (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics analysis described in the manuscript.

claim: The majority of the significantly modulated lipid molecules were identified at the late phase of infection, that is, 7 or 14 dpi serum samples.
source: Interestingly, majority of the significantly modulated lipid molecules were identified at the late phase of infection, that is, 7 or 14 dpi serum samples corroborating with the appearance of CVC in 7 dpi hamster hearts (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by volcano plot analysis presented in Figure 4D.

claim: In total, 275 lipids were differentially regulated in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters, of which 65 lipids molecules were upregulated while 208 were downregulated.
source: In total, 275 lipids were differentially regulated as identified by t-test analysis (described in the 'Materials and methods' section), of which 65 lipids molecules were upregulated while 208 were downregulated as identified by log2 fold change (FC) in volcano plots (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Venn diagram presented in Figure 4E.

claim: Unsaturated TGs (4–11 double bonds), plasmanyl-PE (1–6 db), and plasmanyl-TGs (1–3 db) were uniquely upregulated during SARS-CoV-2 infection in hamsters.
source: Our lipidomics data show that unsaturated TGs (4–11 double bonds [db]), plasmanyl-PE (1–6 db), and plasmanyl-TGs (1–3 db) were uniquely upregulated during infection while saturated TGs (1–3 db), DGs, oxidized lipids, PC, PE, and PI were found to be downregulated during infection.
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics analysis and heatmap data presented in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Saturated TGs (1–3 db), DGs, oxidized lipids, PC, PE, and PI were found to be downregulated during SARS-CoV-2 infection in hamsters.
source: Our lipidomics data show that unsaturated TGs (4–11 double bonds [db]), plasmanyl-PE (1–6 db), and plasmanyl-TGs (1–3 db) were uniquely upregulated during infection while saturated TGs (1–3 db), DGs, oxidized lipids, PC, PE, and PI were found to be downregulated during infection.
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics analysis and heatmap data presented in Figure 4F and G.

claim: LCFA TGs were more abundant in the serum of infected hamsters as compared to uninfected hamsters.
source: Quite remarkably, we found LCFA TGs to be more abundant in the serum of infected hamsters as compared to uninfected hamsters.
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics analysis described in the manuscript.

claim: MCFA TGs were more abundant in uninfected hamsters as compared to infected hamsters.
source: On the contrary, medium-chain fatty acid (MCFA) TGs were more abundant in uninfected hamsters as compared to infected hamsters.
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics analysis described in the manuscript.

claim: Increased LCFAs and decreased MCFAs are associated with increased risks of heart diseases.
source: This corroborated with a previously published report that showed that increased LCFAs and decreased MCFAs are associated with increased risks of heart diseases (Labarthe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Labarthe et al., 2008.

claim: Metabolomic changes are associated with COVID-19 patients.
source: Emerging literature has suggested that metabolomic changes are associated with COVID-19 patients (Bruzzone et al., 2020; Grassin-Delyle et al., 2021; Shen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Bruzzone et al., 2020; Grassin-Delyle et al., 2021; Shen et al., 2020).

claim: t-test analysis followed by FDR correction identified 62 differentially modulated metabolites out of 334 metabolites in hamster serum samples.
source: t-test analysis followed by false discovery rate (FDR) correction identified 62 differentially modulated metabolites out of 334 metabolites in hamster serum samples.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics analysis described in the manuscript.

claim: Out of 62 differentially modulated metabolites, 50 serum metabolites were found to be upregulated while 12 metabolites were found to be downregulated during SARS-CoV-2 infection in hamsters.
source: Out of these 62 differentially modulated metabolites, 50 serum metabolites were found to be upregulated while 12 metabolites were found to be downregulated during infection as compared to uninfected control hamster serum (described in the 'Materials and methods' section) (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics analysis and Venn diagram presented in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Arginine biosynthesis and arginine proline metabolism are the two profoundly modulated metabolic pathways in SARS-CoV-2-challenged hamsters.
source: Furthermore, pathway enrichment analysis revealed that arginine biosynthesis and arginine proline metabolism are the two profoundly modulated metabolic pathways in SARS-CoV-2-challenged hamsters (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by pathway enrichment analysis presented in Figure 5D.

claim: 2 dpi and 14 dpi serum samples showed a higher number of significantly modulated metabolites while 4 dpi serum samples showed no significantly modulated serum metabolites.
source: Quite interestingly, 2 dpi and 14 dpi serum samples showed a higher number of significantly modulated metabolites while 4 dpi serum samples showed no significantly modulated serum metabolites (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by heatmap analysis presented in Figure 5F.

claim: Six metabolites (arginine, N-acetylglutamate, N-acetyl-tryptophan, ornithine, proline, and sphingomyelin) were distinctly common between severe vs. healthy, nonsevere vs. healthy (Shen et al. study), and the hamster serum profile.
source: When compared to COVID-19 serum metabolomics profile data published by Bo Shen et al., we found six metabolites, viz, arginine, N-acetylglutamate, N-acetyl-tryptophan, ornithine, proline, and sphingomyelin, to be distinctly common between severe vs. healthy, nonsevere vs. healthy (Shen et al. study), and the hamster serum profile (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by comparative metabolomics analysis presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Two metabolites (isovalerylglycine and uracil) were uniquely common between severe vs. healthy and hamster profiles.
source: Furthermore, two metabolites were uniquely common between severe vs. healthy and hamster, that is, isovalerylglycine and uracil.
evidence: This is supported by comparative metabolomics analysis presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Five metabolites (5-hydroxyindoleacetate, adenosine, carnitine, fumurate, and propionylcarnitine) were unique between the nonsevere and hamster profiles but were absent in the severe COVID-19 profile.
source: Five metabolites were unique between the nonsevere and hamster profiles but were absent in the severe COVID-19 profile: 5-hydroxyindoleacetate, adenosine, carnitine, fumurate, and propionylcarnitine.
evidence: This is supported by comparative metabolomics analysis presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Only one metabolite, N-acetylneuraminate, overlapped between severe vs. nonsevere COVID-19 profile and was also present in infected hamsters.
source: Only one metabolite, N-acetylneuraminate, overlapped between severe vs. nonsevere COVID-19 profile and was also present in infected hamsters (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by comparative metabolomics analysis presented in Figure 6B and C.

claim: N-acetylneuraminate was uniquely present in the serum of all the COVID-19 patients irrespective of disease pathology, disease stage, or demographical distribution, and was found significantly elevated in the SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters.
source: Among the 14 identified serum metabolites that were common between severe, nonsevere, and infected hamster serum profiles, it was found that only one, N-acetylneuraminate, was uniquely present in the serum of all the COVID-19 patients irrespective of disease pathology, disease stage, or demographical distribution, and was found significantly elevated in the SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by comparative metabolomics analysis presented in Figure 6E.

claim: N-acetylneuraminate had been previously described as CVC biomarkers and is correlated with increased heart risk.
source: Quite interestingly, N-acetylneuraminate had been previously described as CVC biomarkers and is correlated with increased heart risk (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: N-acetylneuraminate is associated with coronary artery disease (CAD) and myocardial injury.
source: In the line with data on CVC, we found an increased serum N-acetylneuraminate, a functional metabolite found to be associated with coronary artery disease (CAD) and myocardial injury (Maciel et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), in the samples of the SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters and COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Maciel et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018).

claim: huACE2 and haACE2 receptors share major sequence homology.
source: This is not surprising as huACE2 and haACE2 receptors have been shown to share major sequence homology (Chan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chan et al., 2020.

claim: Viremia is an important pathological characteristic of SARS-CoV-2 infection in humans.
source: Viremia is an important pathological characteristic of SARS-CoV-2 infection in humans, and further, SARS-CoV-2 is known to shed viral proteins that remain in circulation in the serum long after the virus is cleared, which provide humoral immunity against subsequent strain-specific infection (Atkinson and Petersen, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Atkinson and Petersen, 2020.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is known to shed viral proteins that remain in circulation in the serum long after the virus is cleared, which provide humoral immunity against subsequent strain-specific infection.
source: Viremia is an important pathological characteristic of SARS-CoV-2 infection in humans, and further, SARS-CoV-2 is known to shed viral proteins that remain in circulation in the serum long after the virus is cleared, which provide humoral immunity against subsequent strain-specific infection (Atkinson and Petersen, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Atkinson and Petersen, 2020.

claim: The host responds to pathogenic factors by producing IgG antibodies for effective neutralization.
source: The host responds to these pathogenic factors by producing IgG antibodies for effective neutralization (Rogers et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rogers et al., 2020.

claim: IFNγ, IL-6, and IL-17A were found to be important mediators and the hallmark of acute inflammatory response induced by SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: IFNγ, IL-6, and IL-17A were found to be important mediators and the hallmark of acute inflammatory response induced by SARS-CoV-2 infection (Moore and June, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Moore and June, 2020.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection affects the cardiovascular system, which results in inflammation, endothelial activation, and microvascular thrombosis.
source: Emerging reports suggest that SARS-CoV-2 infection affects the cardiovascular system, which results in inflammation, endothelial activation, and microvascular thrombosis (Giustino et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2020; Nishiga et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Giustino et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2020; Nishiga et al., 2020).

claim: CVC is one of the comorbidities found to be associated with COVID-19 patients.
source: CVC is one of the comorbidities found to be associated with COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is established knowledge about COVID-19 comorbidities.

claim: Serum cTnI is an established prognosis marker for CVC and is associated with an increased risk of heart failure.
source: Serum cTnI is an established prognosis marker for CVC and is associated with an increased risk of heart failure.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cTnI as a biomarker.

claim: Serum lipid molecules are important soluble mediators that are associated with cardiovascular disease.
source: Serum lipid molecules are other important soluble mediators that are associated with cardiovascular disease (Labarthe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Labarthe et al., 2008.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection in hamsters leads to global changes in the lipid profile occurring at 7 and 14 dpi.
source: We found that SARS-CoV-2 infection in hamsters leads to global changes in the lipid profile occurring at 7 and 14 dpi.
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics analysis described in the manuscript.

claim: The hamster model for SARS-CoV-2 has been described as a suitable model to study lung pathologies and their associated clinical parameters.
source: As of now, the hamster model for SARS-CoV-2 has been described as a suitable model to study lung pathologies and their associated clinical parameters (Chan et al., 2020; Imai et al., 2020; Kaptein et al., 2020; Kreye et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020; Osterrieder et al., 2020; Sia et al., 2020; Tostanoski et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection in hamsters can be classified into early and late phases of infection with distinct pulmonary and extrapulmonary pathophysiologies.
source: Our data suggest that SARS-CoV-2 infection in hamsters can be classified into early and late phases of infection with distinct pulmonary and extrapulmonary pathophysiologies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The early phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection in hamsters is characterized by a high lung viral load, lung injury, and an acute inflammatory response.
source: While the early phase of infection is characterized by a high lung viral load, lung injury, and an acute inflammatory response, the late phase of the infection was characterized by the appearance of cardiovascular pathologies and heart-related complications.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The late phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection in hamsters was characterized by the appearance of cardiovascular pathologies and heart-related complications.
source: While the early phase of infection is characterized by a high lung viral load, lung injury, and an acute inflammatory response, the late phase of the infection was characterized by the appearance of cardiovascular pathologies and heart-related complications.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hamsters could serve as a robust preclinical model for understanding pathologies associated with early and late phases of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Together, our study provides the first proof of concept that hamsters could serve as a robust preclinical model for understanding pathologies associated with early and late phases of SARS-CoV-2 infection, and provide a basis to test therapeutics at different phases of SARS-CoV-2 infection-associated early and late pathologies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The hamster model provides a basis to test therapeutics at different phases of SARS-CoV-2 infection-associated early and late pathologies.
source: Together, our study provides the first proof of concept that hamsters could serve as a robust preclinical model for understanding pathologies associated with early and late phases of SARS-CoV-2 infection, and provide a basis to test therapeutics at different phases of SARS-CoV-2 infection-associated early and late pathologies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CVC pathologies in SARS-CoV-2 infection are a consequence of both SARS-CoV-2 infection of heart cells and release of soluble factors.
source: It seems, therefore, that CVC pathologies in SARS-CoV-2 infection are a consequence of both SARS-CoV-2 infection of heart cells and release of soluble factors (Francis et al., 2021), causing CVC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of viral load in the heart and elevated serum markers, supported by a citation to Francis et al., 2021.

claim: The interplay between host-virus interaction via ACE2-RBD and its impact on the host renin-angiotensin system (RAS) and immunological response is central to the development of CVC.
source: The interplay between host-virus interaction via ACE2-RBD and its impact on the host renin-angiotensin system (RAS) and immunological response is central to the development of CVC (Giustino et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Giustino et al., 2020.

claim: Splenomegaly could be used as an indicator of disease severity and cytokine release syndrome in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters.
source: These observations, together, indicated that splenomegaly could be used as an indicator of disease severity and cytokine release syndrome, and thus can be used as one of the key parameters to determine SARS-CoV-2 infection in hamsters.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of splenomegaly correlating with disease progression.

claim: Elevated Foxp-3 expression suggests a suppressive immunological response induced by regulatory T (Tregs) cells was increased with the declining of the infection.
source: However, the transcription factor forkhead box protein (Foxp)-3 was found to be elevated at 14 dpi, suggesting a suppressive immunological response induced by regulatory T (Tregs) cells was increased with the declining of the infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of Foxp-3 in Tregs and its elevated expression at 14 dpi.

claim: Elevated iNOS expression indicates a possible role of an oxidative environment in SARS-CoV-2-induced pathologies.
source: We also found elevated expression of inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) at 2 dpi compared to uninfected hamsters, indicating a possible role of an oxidative environment in SARS-CoV-2-induced pathologies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of iNOS in generating oxidative stress.

claim: Anti-inflammatory cytokines IL-10 and TGF-β could serve to counterbalance an aggressive inflammatory reaction.
source: Interestingly, anti-inflammatory cytokines, IL-10, and transforming growth factor (TGF)-β, set in much early at 2 dpi, which could serve to counterbalance an aggressive inflammatory reaction (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known anti-inflammatory functions of IL-10 and TGF-β.

claim: Upregulation of PD-1 and PDL-1 suggests the induction of checkpoints to suppress the acute immune response induced by SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: In addition, mRNA expression of PD-1 and its ligand, PDL-1, was found to be upregulated at the onset of infection, suggesting the induction of checkpoints to suppress the acute immune response induced by SARS-CoV-2 infection (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of PD-1/PDL-1 in immune checkpoint regulation.

claim: The virus may invade the heart and cause direct infection and injury to cardiomyocytes or it may release soluble mediators in the blood that may cause CVC.
source: It may be possible that the virus invades the heart and causes direct infection and injury to cardiomyocytes or it may release soluble mediators in the blood that may cause CVC.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanisms of CVC based on the observed data.
